utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. The Chamber got the information that you would like to address something about documents, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. President, that's correct, we do have a document. It is P01017, which had some translation issues, I think, when it was used with Mr. Janc, and we do have a completed translation of that document -- English translation of the document that has been up-loaded into e-court. Initially, the document had a partial English translation and only certain pages of it had been translated, so now we have the complete document, and that's from -- I think it's ERN 0677-819 [sic] through 0677-7849, and that's the complete document. We have the translation of all of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is the document you used with Mr. Janc and it is not a document you are going to use with Mr. Blaszczyk?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think it actually is a document that we will use with Mr. Blaszczyk, because it concerns the searches that were executed relative to the materials attributed to General Mladic. And it was used before, on the 22nd of September, during the examination of Mr. Janc, and I believe it's also on Mr. Elderkin's exhibit list to use with Mr. Blaszczyk as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Leave is granted to replace the original, not complete, translation by the complete translation. Now the Chamber would like to issue an oral decision. The Chamber is seized of the Prosecution's supplemental motion for leave to amend its 65 ter list filed on Monday, the 22nd of November. In this motion, the Prosecution seeks the addition of 29 documents related to the so-called Mladic note-books, as well as the additional testimony of OTP Investigator Tomasz Blaszczyk concerning the provenance of these note-books. The day before yesterday, Mr. Gajic indicated that the Defence would not take a position on the motion. The Chamber now delivers its decision. Having reviewed the proposed evidence, the Chamber finds that the 29 documents and the planned testimony are, prima facie, relevant and likely to be of probative value, and that the Prosecution has acted diligently with regard to the proposed additions, showing good cause for the request since these documents came into the possession of the Prosecution only relatively recently. The Chamber, mindful of the Prosecution's duty to present available evidence in seeking to prove its case, also finds that the additions to the 65 ter exhibit list will not result in undue delay or cause prejudice on the accused. For these reasons, the Chamber finds that the proposed additions to the 65 ter lists are in the interests of justice. Accordingly, the motion is granted. Furthermore, given the proposed scheduling of Mr. Blaszczyk for this week, the Chamber would be amenable to a request by the accused to delay his cross-examination of the witness if he needs more time to prepare. If there is nothing else to address, the witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Welcome back to the courtroom. I have to remind you that the solemn declaration that you made at the beginning of your testimony still applies today. Mr. Tolimir is continuing his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May there be peace in this courtroom, and may the hearing today, as well as the proceedings in its totality, be concluded according to God's will and not my own. I'd like to greet the witness, and I wish us all fruitful work today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yesterday, we left off discussing where we discussed the statement. We came to page 32, when you were taken out in the corridor and you were told that you were to go to Orahovac because the prisoners were fleeing. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: To the OTP investigators, on page 31 of your statement, you said as follows -- could we please have that on the screen. It is P1181. Thank you, Aleksandar. We have page 31 now. Please look at lines 12 to 25. You say: "No, I don't know. They just picked me up at Standard, telling me that people were trying to escape from Orahovac. I picked up my M-48 and went out. I came out because they saw me in the corridor. Had I not been there, I would not have gone to Orahovac." I guess that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "And so I boarded a small truck that was parked in the compound, and then we went to that place. And the reason why they took me, they said they are running away. So that was a pretext ..." et cetera. In this part of your statement, you describe those events. This is my question: Did anyone order you to go to Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in the narrow sense of the words. I was just told that we should pick up a weapon because the prisoners were fleeing, but it wasn't strictly an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you in uniform at the time?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm waiting for the transcript. If someone comes across a soldier in the street, and if that person was a civilian, telling the soldier that the prisoners were fleeing, would that soldier go to the location because he felt obliged to do so?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does it sound logical to you that if someone tells you that prisoners are escaping, you would not refuse to carry out such an order or to follow up on that proposition?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe at that time I believed I should go. I can't really be precise. I wasn't too clear about it then, and it's not very clear to me today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that it's difficult to recall it so many years later. Let us move on to page 31, lines 29 and 30. It's on the same page, towards the bottom. And it's page 32 in the English, the first paragraph. There, you say how you got off the truck in the courtyard and someone indicated two corpses to you that were covered, and they were already putrefying. You say that their hands were already getting black. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So did you see those people being killed?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 37 in the Serbian, you again repeat your description of how you were told to pick up your weapon to go to Orahovac in order to try to prevent the prisoners from escaping. It is lines 10 to 14 in the Serbian, page 37. Have a look at the page, please. In the English, it's page 37, the last paragraph. My question is: Later on, when you described the situation, when you were told to pick up your gun, the investigators had numerous questions about that, and then in lines 28 to 30, they say: "Am I right in saying that when the people who worked with you there knew -- whether they knew that all of the prisoners would be taken away ..." Those were the words of the OTP investigator. It's page 38 in English.

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did any of you who went to Orahovac know that the Muslims fleeing from Srebrenica would be captured and taken to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could anyone know that the Muslims would try to break through, with the assistance of arms, through the territory of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did the population around Orahovac know that all prisoners were to be taken to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. How could they have known?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecutor put some questions to you here, when they showed you some photographs, and first you marked the location of the two corpses that you saw of the killed Muslims. That was page 56 of yesterday's transcript. You indicated that they were close to the fence. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Then you said that - and that was page 58 and 59 - you saw Drago and Vujadin Popovic.

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were they there throughout the time when you were there?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't there the whole time, myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But while you were there?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were there at that point in time, but how long they stayed there, that is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you see who negotiated with the Muslims to board the vehicles, telling them that they were to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that in the yard. Drago Nikolic organised it, but they didn't want to go. They resisted it. And then Drago was supposed to go there to negotiate with them, and he promised them they would be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is: Did you take part in those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: At page 63 of yesterday's transcript, and page 65 as well as 67, you were asked by the Prosecutor whether you saw that boy next to the gym, escorted by a soldier. Later on, at page 65, the Prosecutor asks how many children you saw around the school, and you said that you were positive you saw one.

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I think the Prosecutor asked you that because at page 32 of your statement - could we please have that - in line 27, you said: "When I was seated there, I saw two children."

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is this why the Prosecutor asked you about that, because you mentioned two children in your statement?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I tried to explain yesterday. There could have been two or only that one, but when I was sitting down, I saw a boy with a bucket, and then when I was in the yard, I saw a boy again, but I don't know whether it's the same boy, the one I saw at the stairs of the cultural hall and later on in the yard. But at least I'm positive I saw one child.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So as you told the Prosecutor yesterday, you were certain you saw at least one child.

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I can't say anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That's why I'm putting this question to you. It was based on your statement, and that's why you were asked about that yesterday. You say you saw one.

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's certain.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 40. Page 42 in the English, the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm asking you about this because yesterday they asked you whether you were in the gym, itself, in Orahovac. You only mentioned the negotiations. Hence, I'm asking you this: Did you see the Muslim prisoners in the gym or not?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move to page 41, lines 1 to 7. We can see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You describe how your M-48 rifle got jammed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you manage to fix it when you were in Orahovac? Did you try to cock it subsequently?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I didn't even load it on that day. There was no need.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When did you manage to fix it?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Who was present then? Because you also said that a weapons expert was there.

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Jerkic, Ljubisa, I think. He simply hit it on the breach and then a piece of paper slid out. That's what caused the jam.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does this prove that you basically did not use your weapon while you were in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to me, that's proof enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So you could not have been an accomplice, because you were accused of that.

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never realised that I was accused of being that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to that question. It obviously calls for a legal conclusion, which this witness is not qualified to make. I think Mr. Tolimir is perfectly aware of that, and I would ask him to refrain from putting legal questions to this witness. The question of whether or not he's an accomplice or not in relation to an execution has more to do -- had more than to do with simply firing his weapon. I mean, I think Mr. Tolimir -- General Tolimir is perfectly aware of that. It's an inappropriate question to put to this witness, and I think that General Tolimir is intentionally trying to distort the record of these proceedings on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I simply wanted the witness to tell the Court whether he fired or not and when the gun was fixed, which was after the events. It's part of the record now, and it is up to you to attach whatever importance to it is necessary. I won't pursue this line of questions because I see that the Prosecution objects. We will move on to page 57 of your statement. Could we please have that in e-court, which is page 60 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In lines 16 and 17, you again describe having seen two killed persons, two corpses, next to the fence, and you indicated their location on the school photograph yesterday. My question is this, if you can recall it: Were these the only corpses you saw in the school compound, on the pitch in front of the school and the gym?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these were the only two corpses I saw in the proximity of the gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The fact that their hands were black, as the others had seen as well, does that indicate that they were killed before you arrived?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were certainly killed before I arrived. But when, exactly, and how, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know why their hands were of such a dark colour?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was just the impression I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know that hands can be dark from hemorrhaging after death or because they had been strung up?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's just the impression I had, and I mentioned it in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You did in lines 28 and 29, and you did so again. Can we now see page 73 in e-court. We will see it now. In English, it's lines 10 to 15, page 79. I will read a part of what you said to demonstrate the degree of your goodwill or lack of goodwill to go there: "What we said, that people who were detained wanted to escape --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot find this. Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, first, please slow down. And, secondly, indicate where you are reading from, because the interpreters didn't find this part of the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 79, first paragraph in English. And it's lines 10 to 15, page 73, in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I repeat: "Well, no, it was said that we should go there, as we said, that people were about to escape, those who were detained, and it's easy to give in. It's not that I was spurred to go there, but simply -- I mean, what if people really wanted to escape? Okay, you don't have to go, but then it's chaos. 1.200 people, they can really do God knows what. I thought it was possible. I mean, it was said that it was possible." Did you really believe that the Muslim prisoners were about to escape?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believed it when they said it, that they were really going to escape.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: May a soldier, in war, refuse anyone's demand or summons to prevent the escape of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what to say to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you don't want to speak about it, I'm not going to ask anymore. Tell us only what you want to talk about, and I'm going to ask you only about that. Now, can we move to page 94. While we're waiting, I'd like to ask you something else. It's page 100 in English. Did you state to the Prosecution that you had not participated in the activities at Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That's correct. I'm sorry, I said this before I quoted. In lines 24 through 30, on page 94, you say: "Well, simply, I did not take part in it, as far as these executions in Orahovac or anywhere are concerned. I never did any harm to anyone, and I had no reason to cause harm to anyone, and I tried in every possible way to avoid doing so, beginning with 1992 and in Orahovac as well. What else? Well, the only problem is that all these accusations and all of a sudden you are suspected, without any real proof, I don't know, and it turns out I'm guilty without a conviction." And then the Prosecutor tells you: "So the reason you are indicated as a suspect is the report we received that you had been present ..." That's page 101 in English: " ... is the report we received that you were present in the area of Orahovac on the day when the people were killed." And then on page 95, in line 5, the same investigator of the OTP tells you: "You were on the crime scene, and our question was whether you had taken part in it, and that's why you were invited here as a suspect." My question to you is: During the interrogation by the investigators of the OTP, did you state anything that would be contrary to what you stated in the interview in the lines 24 through 30 that I quoted?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did you ask? Did I what?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Say anything contrary to your statement in lines 24 through 30 on this page, that you did not participate in anything and avoided anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I avoided getting involved in every way possible, to the best of my ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: During the interrogation 10 years after the fact, did the investigator ask you to recollect all these events to the best of your ability, and did you answer to the best of your ability?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that now. I probably answered, to the best of my recollection, all the questions they asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the course of the interview, did you conceal or cover up the activities of others, like in the questions about those children, the fact that Muslims were taken to that hill?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why you're asking me this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I meant to say: Did you only talk about what you were sure of?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked only about the things that I was sure of, mainly. And you can see from this interview, and the interpretation is correct -- you can see from this interview that I was unsure, I didn't know what to say, I had a lot of dilemmas at the time, and somebody asked me why I didn't mention any names, and that's -- that's how I behaved, conditionally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In yesterday's transcript, when the summary was being read by Mr. Vanderpuye, he said that you had seen -- and I don't know if it was open session, so I won't say the name -- that you had seen that van driver with a certain group of people, enumerated the people, and you recognised the boy you had seen earlier in the yard at Orahovac, in the school-yard at Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not exactly how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Tell us how it was, then.

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that interview, that first interview, I did not speak about the driver or the people who were there with him. Right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, the second time, when I was a Defence witness in the Blagojevic and Jokic case, I mentioned it because some other people did not want to come to the courtroom to at least try to help Jokic, because I don't know Blagojevic that well, so I named the crew of the van, and the boy in the van is not the same boy who carried water. It's not the same boy. And perhaps we should correct one thing. Yesterday, when Miladin Mijakovic [Realtime transcript read in error "Mladen Jekovic"] was mentioned, the Prosecutor said "Mladen." Perhaps the name should be corrected. And the boy said, when the van approached Standard, Is this Srebrenica? Where's my father? The boy said that when he saw the lights lit. That would be a correct quotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for this correction. That's on transcript pages 7982 to 7985. I don't know what happened in open session and what happened in private session, so I have to be careful. Now, tell us, since the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber know what you just said, they know what you said where, what you said in open session and private session - I won't go into it - just tell me: What time was it when you got into that van that carried the boy?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was speaking roughly because I can't be precise; I didn't have a watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Sorry, I want to remind you: The summary said it was about 6.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then it must be around that time, perhaps half an hour later. It could be between -- between 10.00 and 12.00. I believe we arrived at Standard before 12.00, before midnight, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Two things. First, I think the summary is in the record, and it doesn't refer to 6.00 but, I think, between 10.30 and 11.00 or something like that. The second thing is: On page 15, at line 12, the witness was correcting the name Miladin Mijatovic. It's recorded in the transcript at "Mladen Jekovic," so I think that should be corrected as well so that the record is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, you corrected a name. Can you repeat the correct name again, please, of this person Miladin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It should be Miladin, M -i-l-a-d-i-n, Mijatovic, not Mladen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And, Mr. Tolimir, can you clarify the time? I think now a contradiction in the answer of the witness, you should discuss with the witness again the time which you took from the summary. And you see the witness said it must be around that time, and then later he referred to the time between 10.00 and 12. You should clarify that with the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. It's best for the witness to answer my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you say, for the record, when you got into the van that you hitched -- that picked you up on the road from Orahovac to your barracks, Standard? Just tell us exactly whether it was in the morning or afternoon.

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was around 11.00 p.m. I'm just trying to remember. I mean, you all want precision, and I can't say exactly what time it was because I didn't have a watch. But let's take it that it was around 2300 hours that I got into that van.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Now the witness said, for the record, it was around 2300 hours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And even that is a supposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You shouldn't fear that you are going to have any problems because of this. Just tell us if there is anyone who can confirm that, and how many such people.

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the people who were in the van, and Mira Vidovic, who I went to see after I got out of the van.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What's important for us is the people who were in the van, whether they can confirm it.

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, and Mira Vidovic, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But she cannot know how long you had been waiting for that van.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm not sure, but I think there may be a translation issue with respect to what the witness said at page 17, lines 20 through 21, where he says: "Well, the people who were in the van," obviously can confirm when he was in it, "and Mira Vidovic, who I went to see after I got out of the van." And I think there may be a translation error with respect to that. If the witness could clarify it, I think that would be better, because in the chronology of his prior testimony he would have left her house before he got into the van. So that becomes an issue in and of itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Tanic, can you help us with this? When did you see Mira - what was her name? - Vidovic? Before you entered the van or after you have left the van?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I left her house and went to the road, as I stated earlier. I thought first I would walk, and then it seemed too far away and unsafe, so I stopped 50 metres away from her house, waiting for someone I know to pass by. And I knew a lot of people, and this van came by. I left Mira's house, I don't know at what time, I can't be precise, and then I waited for someone who could take me to Standard. This van came by. They first passed me by, and then they stopped and then they backed up. I got in, and that van took me to Standard. So Mira can confirm at what time I left her house. I cannot be sure about the time. Of course, I had spent a lot of time sitting in her house. That's not in dispute. But she can confirm only when I left, and those in the van can confirm when they stopped to pick me up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this clarification. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tanic. I'm sorry we are taking so long over such a detail. What's important to me is that there are people in the van who can confirm you were not in Orahovac at that time, but you were getting into the van.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is that a question? Is that a question for the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I asked the witness if there were any people who can confirm when he got into the van, that he didn't get into the van from the school-yard but from the street.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there are such people. Mira can confirm, and these who were in the van. They can confirm that I got into the van, but not from the school-yard.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. I have no further questions for you. Thank you for testifying, and thank you for all your answers. I'm sorry if I angered you in any way. Thank you, Mr. President. I've concluded my cross-examination. I wish the witness a safe journey. God bless you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Vanderpuye, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Tanic, again. I just wanted to clarify a few issues with you. First, we've been talking about when it was that you got into the van or when it was that you left Ms. Vidovic's house. I just want to point out, first of all, to you that in the summary that I read into the record, I did not mention 6.00 at all. It's not anywhere in the summary. In fact, what is mentioned there, and maybe you can confirm this, is that you remained at your friend's house, Mira Vidovic's house, until about 10.00 or 11.00 p.m. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But in total, I was in her house for seven or six hours. That's the total time I spent in her house; a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. You left there somewhere around 10.00 -- or between 10.00 and 11.00 p.m. on 14 July 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That should be right. Again, I'm saying I can't be sure or precise about the time and the hour when I left Mira's house, but I suppose so. And when I said six hours, it's the time I spent in her house, in Mira's house. It could be even seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. You were asked several questions about the child that you saw at the school, and I believe you indicated that you saw at least one child there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One for sure.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would appreciate it if the Prosecutor could say that he didn't see the child in the school but in the yard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. One carried water, and the other boy was on the pitch. That's where I saw him. Whether the other boy also carried water, I'm not sure. In any case, when I was sitting on the steps outside the cultural hall, a boy was carrying a bucket of water, escorted by one soldier, and then I saw him again when I was about to leave. Near Mira's house, a boy was passing by the pitch with a bucket. Whether it was the same boy or there were two boys, I don't know. In any case, there were some children. One of the reasons I got angry is I was thinking, Are they going to execute these children too?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think the matter is quite clear now, as it was earlier. The problem arose by the use of the words that "you saw at the school." And, Mr. Tolimir, perhaps that is a translation issue again. In your question, you said "in the school," but that was not the word Mr. Vanderpuye used. Please carry on, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is it your -- is it your judgement or your recollection, Mr. Tanic, that at the school or on the pitch, or the vicinity of the school, that there were only two children there on that day? And when I mean children, I mean Muslim children, the ones whom you thought might be executed.

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether I saw one or two, is that what you're asking? I said here before -- because everything you say here is a problem, it seems -- I can't be sure. I saw one boy carrying water when I was sitting on the steps outside the cultural hall. And then when I was walking along that road where Cedo Jovic and others were, I saw a boy with a bucket on the pitch, also carrying water. Whether it's the same boy or two different boys, I don't know. But in any case, I saw two boys, the one in the van and the one carrying water. Let's say that I saw one near the pitch or behind the cultural hall carrying water, to be -- I mean, I can't claim anything with any certainty. I can't be sure now. Maybe it's one-and-the-same boy that I saw twice, once behind the cultural hall and once passing by the pitch. That's the best I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... your answer, but it's not the answer to the question that I asked you. My question was: Is it your judgement that there were only those children that you saw at the school, in the vicinity of the school, on that day while you were there? That's my question, and that's a bit different than --

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say anything for sure. I did not go into the gym, and I don't know. But even if there were only two, that's enough. I did not go into the gym, however, and I didn't ask anyone later whether -- I mean, I can only suppose there were some, but suppositions are not good enough. I told you what I saw, and I didn't go into the gym, and I don't know if there were any more children. I did not ask the others later whether there were more boys or not. I did not ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I put the question in the following way: I'm not referring to the gym and the people inside of the gym. Did you see at that time other young men or boys outside the building in the vicinity of the school, others --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... one or two boys carrying water?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there weren't any other children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: During your testimony, both this time around and in the Popovic case, you indicated that you were concerned about these children, in fact. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't think it was right. The boy I saw could have been as old as my children, and then if I tried to imagine that someone had to kill my children, it wasn't right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In the Popovic case, you were asked about this issue, and this is at page 1345, lines 24 down. It's P1177. You were asked the following question and you gave this answer: "Would you tell us what it was that you found revolting." And your answer was: "Well, because, conditionally speaking, it was obvious that there would be some organisation. There was no question of transport, and there were children there as well." Do you recall giving the answer to that question concerning what you saw when you were at the -- or in the vicinity of the school on 14 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. That is why I'm trying to say things from memory again. Perhaps it was just one child. But in any case, throughout the three or four hours, I saw two boys, one in the van, one carrying water. So there were children there. And going any further would serve no use. I did suppose that there were more children. And then they said, Well, they'll grow up. And I couldn't comprehend that way of thinking. I found it offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you say, They would say, They'll grow up, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in case they would be released, later on when they grew up, they would wage war again. That was the sense, I think: If we allow them to grow up, then there would be trouble, and someone took the right to deny them that. I stand by the same things I said then, but, of course, I will never use the exactly same words. There would be differences, always, and then there's always a problem, whether I said this or that, in what sequence, et cetera. But in essence, I think I'm saying the same thing. As for how I put it depends on the question, the situation, et cetera. In any case, the statements I provided before and what I'm saying today are all basically the same. I did not change anything that was important. I explained the things the way I saw them. There is the 2002 statement, which is somewhat confusing, as I have tried to explain. I didn't know what to say, what not to say, how to behave. No one was telling me anything, I was simply left to my own devices. Perhaps I should have had an attorney, but I don't think I would have fared much better in that case either.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't mean to interrupt you, but my question was simply: What do you mean when you say, They will grow up, that somebody told you, They will grow up? I think you've answered that, and I'll ask you a different question. You referred on a number of occasions to children in your testimony in the Popovic case; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you were asked a question by General Tolimir. I'm not sure exactly what page it is on the transcript, but you will recall that he referred to the putrefying hands or bodies of the two individuals you saw covered in the school-yard. Do you remember that? I see that it's at page 5, and it's lines 20 through 23.

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You were asked for an explanation about why these hands appeared to you to be black. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, I don't know. I don't know what I said in the Popovic case. In any case, I stand by what I said before and today, in the main points, although my way of presenting it may differ from one situation to the next. Perhaps there I said that, if I could remember correctly, their hands were covered in dust and dirt. But, in any case, they seemed black to me. I don't know why, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. And, in fact, you said, during your interview in 2002, 24 June 2002 -- I have it as P1181, I have it here as page 34 in the English, and you said precisely that: "I saw their hands were black. Maybe it was dust or something." Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible. I suppose so. I can't say anything for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, you can say what you said before, can't you?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You mentioned that you did not see prisoners in the gym on cross-examination today. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see them in the gym. I didn't approach the gym nor enter it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you arrived at the gym -- I mean, at the school, itself, you were outside the fence that you indicated in the photographs that I presented you yesterday; right?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And from the fence, you can see the entrance to the gym, you can see the gym building; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you know that there were prisoners in the school during the period of time -- in the school or in the gym, during the period of time when you were there, without having seen them?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see them, but they were in the gym, and at the door there were soldiers standing guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: How did you know they were in the gym if you didn't see them?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because when I came to the road, I could hear the clamour. The sound was like that of a beehive being close by. They were talking, and then I knew they were there because the boy was carrying water, or there may have been two boys, I don't know anymore. How did I know? Well, there was -- there were clothes on the road, there were two corpses in the yard; that's how I knew. And, lastly, there were the military policemen there, guarding them. They told me how many there were, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You also knew because you saw them getting loaded onto a truck; isn't that right, Mr. Tanic?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the way I stated: I only saw when they were being put onto the first truck. I didn't pay much attention to it later. I wasn't following it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, may I put an additional question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You just said, in one of your answers, and I quote: "And, lastly, there were the military policemen there, guarding them. They told me how many there were ..." et cetera. End of quote. What did they tell you about the number of people, number of prisoners in the gym?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of them, or someone along the road when I was there, conditionally speaking, they said that there were about 1200. I didn't know anything else. That's the information I got from one of them or some of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Just now, the Prosecutor asked you the following question: "You also knew because you saw them getting loaded onto a truck; isn't that right, Mr. Tanic?" And you answered: "It's the way I stated: I only saw them when they were being put on the first truck." Where did this happen? Where did you see this?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a truck parked at the side entrance of the gym. That's where they were being loaded. I could see two or three of them, but I couldn't make them out, I couldn't recognise them. I repeat that it all seemed so surreal, it seemed as if I were observing the scene through binoculars turned the wrong way. It all seemed far away. It simply didn't occur to me what to do, how to do it. I just saw people being loaded onto the truck, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, this concludes your examination here in this trial. The Chamber would like to thank you that you were able to come to The Hague again and to assist us, and you are now free to return to your normal life and your normal activities. Thank you very much again, and the court usher will assist you leaving the courtroom. Goodbye and thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Goodbye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I see you on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I am indeed, Mr. President. Thank you. We are prepared to proceed with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Elderkin. Welcome to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you. And I hope that following this morning's ruling, we can continue straight with the proposed additional testimony of Mr. Blaszczyk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. He has already entered the courtroom. Welcome to the courtroom again, Mr. Blaszczyk. May I remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth you made at the beginning of your testimony a long time ago still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin has a different set of questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And if I may begin, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Elderkin, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Blaszczyk. As you know, I'm Rupert Elderkin, and the subject of your testimony today concerns how the OTP both obtained and authenticated certain wartime note-books written by General Ratko Mladic, as well as other materials obtained at the same time. And I'd like to begin by asking you about a first search which took place in 2008. Can you tell us the date when the first of General Mladic's note-books were found?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first search of house of General Mladic family was conducted on the 4th December 2008 in Belgrade, and at that time the five note-books of General Mladic were seized in this location.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you know the specific address of that location and whose house it actually was?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The house is located in Belgrade. It's on the street Blagoja Parovica 117A, and this house is -- the owner of this house is Bosiljka Mladic, the wife of General Mladic. And his son, Darko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Who carried out the search? I don't need individual names, but which authorities?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The search was carried out by the MUP unit from Serbia, by the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could we please see P1017, which hopefully by now has the full English translation also available.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: The document that you can see on the screen, Mr. Blaszczyk, can you tell us what this is?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is certificate of temporarily-seized items from the house of Bosiljka Mladic. And I find this receipt of the seized material of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And can you tell us the date you see on the document?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date of this document is 4 December 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: So that's the date the search and seizure actually took place?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. It's the date when the seizure took place, and this document was prepared on the spot at the house of Bosiljka Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And we can see, starting from about halfway down the page, some numbered items. It seems to be a list. What would have listed here?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, we have listed the items seized during the search of this house in Blagoja Parovica 117A in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And can we go to the next page, please. And, I think, actually, one more page in the English so we can get to the end of the document. The B/C/S is two pages, but the English, I think, runs into three.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And at the bottom of this document, there are signatures on the left-hand and right-hand sides. Is there any signature there from a member of the Mladic family?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I recognise the signature on the left-hand side of this document, of the original document, I recognise the signature of Bosiljka Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And can we now go to page 19 in the B/C/S and page 22 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And, again, can you tell us what date you see on this document and what this document is, please.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is dated 12 December 2008, and this is certificate of temporarily-seized items. In fact, this is kind of the review of receipt of the seized items which were seized on the 4th December 2008 at Bosiljka Mladic house. This document was prepared on the building of MUP, and we see in this document we have listed items which, if you look at the previous document -- can we go back to the previous document, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Go back to page 1 in both languages, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we go to the last page of this document -- the previous document, the 4th December 2008 document --

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Okay. That would be page 2 in the B/C/S and page 3 in the English again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We see -- on this English translation, under number 32 and 35, we see: "One sealed carton box contained unchecked written documents." And the same in regards to item number 35. And in the following document, which we saw just a few seconds ago from 12 December 2008, we have receipt of the documents which contain -- which were contained in these two -- in the box of -- listed here as Box 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: So the document we have on the screen was prepared on the day items were taken at the house, and the second document we just saw is a more detailed list of those items a few days later; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. At the time when the search was conducted, the police officer, they had no time to list all these documents that were seized in the house of Bosiljka Mladic. They packed all these documents in a carton box, and later on, on the 12th of December -- in fact, it took place in a few days in December, between 10 and 16 December, in the presence of Darko Mladic, the son of General Ratko Mladic, and his lawyer, they reviewed this document, they prepared a list of the documents seized in the house of Bosiljka Mladic on the 4 December 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the items on the list we have on the screen at the moment include a number of note-books which are on the Prosecution's 65 ter list. In order to be able to make sense of things more easily, I would propose passing up to the Bench and also to the Defence - I provided a copy in B/C/S yesterday - simply a correlation list which lists our 65 ter numbers and the inventory list number as we see here, because we'll be referring between lists, and I think having one on the screen and one in hard copy is the easiest way to proceed, with your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please. The parties, the Bench, and the witness have received this document. At this point in time, Judge Nyambe would like to put a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Blaszczyk, at page 31 of the transcript, you have stated: "I recognise the signature on the left-hand side of this document, of the original document. I recognise the signature of Bosiljka Mladic." How did you become familiar with this signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seen the signature several times in -- during the review of material seized on this house in 2008 and also 2010. And from the report of Serbian MUP, they mentioned that this is Bosiljka Mladic signature. And I can read Cyrillic a little bit, and, in fact, this is the name, "B. Mladic." I can recognise the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'd like to refer just back to the hand-out that has been passed around the courtroom. This appears as 65 ter 6825 on the Prosecution's list of exhibits. Mr. Blaszczyk, if you could look at the hand-out you have in front of you and refer to Table A, please, the 4th of December 2008 search. Can you identify the five note-books taken on that date from the Mladic family home and reference them to the inventory list that we have just seen on the screen? If we could actually have that back up on the screen, that would help.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can identify, but I believe we should go to the following page of this receipt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the meantime, I would ask Mr. Elderkin for a clarification. What do you mean by: "This appears at 65 ter 6825 on the Prosecution's list of exhibits"? Do you mean this compilation has such a number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, yes. This is a demonstrative exhibit that was created for ease of reference, so in due course I would actually seek to tender this item and it's loaded up into e-court. It's simply handed out in the paper copy because of the problems of showing more than one thing at once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was wrong, Your Honour. Your Honour, these first -- these first two note-books are listed on the first page of this document from December 12, 2008. And the first one, this is on this English translation and on original document. It's listed as item number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Which 65 ter number is that, for the record?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Serbian receipt, it's mentioned here as one blue workbook with 27 textual pages, and I recognise this is -- in our list, we described this note-book as blue business note-book with 27 pages of handwritten notes in Cyrillic from 15 September 1992 until 4 October 1992. This is the first note-book which we recognised the handwriting of General Ratko Mladic. And another one from this page is listed here as number 7, one note-book reading "Svila Celinac" with 10 textual pages. And this note-book is listed in our list as one note-book containing written pages regarding 1st September 1993, speech by Ratko Mladic in Banja Luka, and this note-book has our 65 ter number 05489.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And for the record, the first note-book you mentioned, listed as the MUP number 6, does that have the 65 ter number 05487?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct, 05487.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I see the time, Your Honours. I see no problem with breaking now. We can continue with the next items in the next page after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. We will adjourn for the first break and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Elderkin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Blaszczyk, I'd like to continue along the same list from where we left off before the break. I think the same page is visible in e-court, and we'd just finished describing 65 ter numbers 5487 and 5489. So if you could continue with that list, please.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I described already two note-books from this receipt. It's the 65 ter number note-book is 05487 and 05489. And now to look at another note-book, we should go to the following page. On the English translation at item number 8, we have: "One brown leather agenda, reading 'Nis.'" This is note-book I identified as brown leather agenda consisting of handwritten notes covering 27 January 1995 through 5 September 1995. This note-book has our 65 ter number 05490. And under item 11, number 11 on this original receipt, and the English translation, in fact, on the following page of original receipt, we have: "One workbook with red covers." It's our note-book with 65 ter number 05488, one business note-book with red cover, "Radna Beleznica," containing handwritten notes from 20 January 1993 until 31st March 1993. And under number 17, we have the last note-book from this batch. This is our 65 ter number 05486. This is brown business diary with 30 pages of handwritten notes, including notes of the Assembly session held on 14 and 15 September 1992, and conversation with General Philippe Morillon on 27 September 1992. These five note-books were seized at the location of Bosiljka Mladic on the 4th December 2008, at her house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Okay. And could we now go to the next page of this inventory list, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can you tell us whose signatures are at the bottom of this page?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the original last page of this receipt, we see, on the left-hand bottom we have -- we see -- we see the signature of Darko Mladic and lawyer Zara Tijanic. Tijanic Jeftovic. And this, as I said before, this box containing these documents were opened on 12 December 2008 at the premises of MUP in Belgrade, and Darko Mladic was present during the opening of this box and during the listing of all these documents which were inside the box, and he confirmed that this box contained these particular documents with his signature here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And do you specifically recognise his signature or is that based on the typed name that appears above the signature, where it says, in type: "Citizen, Darko Mladic"?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not like in the case of Bosiljka Mladic, that I even recognise the letters, Cyrillic letters, but that one, the signature I seen also several time in other documents. And also the signature is mentioned in the MUP report that this is Darko Mladic signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can you tell us now how this material came into the hands of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this first search which was conducted on the 4th December 2008, we received -- I mean, the OTP received the information about the search from the Serbian authorities in February 2009. And on the 25th February of 2009, OTP -- in fact, our field office in Belgrade, received a digitalised copy of all scanned material you said -- seized at that time at the house of Bosiljka Mladic. This is first time, in fact, we received the copy of the material. It was an electronic copy of the material seized in the house. And later on we asked, in March 20 -- we asked the authority -- the Serbian authority to get access to this original material, and personally me and two of my colleagues went to Belgrade to see this original material. And when we reviewed the original material seized on the 4th December 2008, I selected these five note-books and also, I believe, four videotapes which I considered at that time as the priority material, and immediately we requested this material to be provided to us. And on 27 March 2009, I personally collected these five note-books and plus four videotapes from Serbian deputy war crimes prosecutor in Belgrade. And this material, since 27 March 2009, was exclusively in my possession until 30 March 2009, when I submitted this material to our evidence unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And was there any other original material from that first search which came into the OTP's possession?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was another material -- a lot of material, including videotapes, including documents, but this material we received later on, I think beginning on the 7 of April the same year, 2009. And also I was personally involved in transfer of these documents to The Hague. I went to Belgrade, and on the 7 of April, 2009, we received from the -- also from the deputy war crime prosecutor from Belgrade the entire material. We packed in diplomatic pouch and we transported -- together with my colleague from the field office, I transported this material to The Hague, and also I submitted this material to the evidence unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I want to ask for one correction. I see at page 38 at line 2, you referred to the search being conducted on, and it's written "the 4th of September 2008."

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could you say on what time is the correct date for that first search?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the correct date, of course, is 4th of December, 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And now can we talk, please, about the second search. At some time after the first search, there was another search. Can you tell us when that was?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second search, when the material was seized also on the house of Bosiljka Mladic, was conducted on 23 February 2010.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And, again, that's the same address as the first search?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the search was conducted at the same address in Belgrade, at her house on Blagoja Parovica Street 117A.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Who conducted that search?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the previous search, this search was conducted also by the members of police of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What kind of materials were found during that second search?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the second search -- during the second search conducted on 23 February 2010, the police officer discovered in the house of Bosiljka Mladic more note-books which appeared to be Ratko Mladic note-books, altogether 17 note-books, and more -- more documents, some medical material and video material and audiotapes also containing intercepted conversation, various intercepted conversation. But between material seized at that time on 23 February 2010, there was also 17 note-books which appeared to be General Ratko Mladic note-books.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you have any information as to why this material hadn't been found during the first search?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our information, the first search, the material discovered during the first search, was available on the plain view for the police officers. But this material from 23 February 2010, especially the note-books, they were hidden -- maybe not hidden, but at least not available from the plain view but was -- was -- the material, the 17 note-books, were located in two places. One place, it was in the bedroom of the house, and another part of the note-books were located on the attic, which was accessible only through the bathroom of this apartment or house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could we see, please, 65 ter 6827.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: First, what date do you see on this document?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is dated 23 February 2010, and this document was prepared on -- at the location of Blagoja Parovica 117A Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: So prepared at the house where the search took place?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. This document was prepared at the house where the search was conducted at that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And, again, we see, in the B/C/S version, a handwritten list. That's also, obviously, translated into English. What are the items that are handwritten in this list?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the list of items seized at this location at Blagoja Parovica 117A apartment from Bosiljka Mladic on the 23 February 2010.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And could we just scroll through page by page to see that list through to the end, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Okay. Could you again look towards the bottom of this page and tell us if you recognise any of the signatures there.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the original page, we see that this is signature of Bosiljka Mladic, the same signature which appeared to be on the receipt from 4th December 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Now, if you could look at the hand-out -- the paper hand-out that I passed around the courtroom earlier, and look at Table B, the 23rd of February, 2010 search. This lists, by 65 ter number, a number of documents, followed by a column with "MUP inventory list number" and a description, and, finally, an ERN. Do the 65 ter numbers listed here, to your knowledge, correspond to the inventory list that we're seeing before us?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I checked it, and they correspond to the -- even to the list we see in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Unless Your Honours would like to do so, I wouldn't propose to read through these one by one. I think the correspondence is clear from the hand-out and, obviously, by correlation with the document we have on the screen which is already part of an admitted exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And everybody is in a position to check it for himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Exactly. I would ask at this stage, though, Your Honours, to tender the hand-out formally as Prosecution 65 ter 6825.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I wonder if this is on the Prosecution's exhibit list we received before this testimony. I didn't find it here. Perhaps you can help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: It should be on the third page, I think, of the exhibit list, very close to the end. 6825.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, I see it. Thank you very much. It will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1388, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And also the -- I'm sorry, when I said that the exhibit we had on the screen, the inventory list, had been admitted, I was incorrectly referring to the first list we saw relating to the 2008 search. So the list that we've just been looking at is 65 ter 6827, and I'd also ask for that to be admitted. And, again, that's also on our -- the list circulated before Mr. Blaszczyk's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's right. This will be admitted into evidence too.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1389, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Blaszczyk, do you know if General Mladic's wife marked any of the note-books seized on the 23rd of February, 2010, before they were taken away by the MUP?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In this search conducted on 23 February 2010, Bosiljka Mladic, the wife of General Mladic, she insisted to paginate all these note-books, and also she confirmed the number of the pages at the end of the note-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could we see 65 ter 6811, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Blaszczyk, while this is loading up, you could refer to the paper hand-out, 65 ter 6811, and confirm the description of the note-book we're now seeing on the screen. Can you just tell us what it says there, please?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. This is -- this is in our list 65 ter 06811, this is handwritten note-book of Ratko Mladic covering the period from 27 May 1992 to 31st July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And we can see, on the Table B, that the MUP inventory list number is number 40, and does that correspond, then, to what we see on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the list in front of me, but it corresponds.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And if we could again scroll through the first few pages of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And when you see them, if you could indicate, where are the numbers added by General Mladic's wife?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If -- if we see the first page with handwritten notes on it, and the number is visible on the right-hand corner of the page with -- it was used, I believe, green ink.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And if we could click onto the next page, please, to see that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And we see number 2 also marked by green ink on the left top corner of the page, of the original page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, could we go to the final page of the document. And then once we're at the final page in English and in B/C/S, if we could then start coming back towards the front of the book page by page until we see the first handwriting. I think we need to see the English page 400. I'm not sure -- I think it's page 399 we're seeing, so if we could go one page further in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And can you tell us, what bit is this writing here? Whose handwriting is that?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I mentioned a few minutes ago, that this is confirmation signed by Bosiljka Mladic that this particular diary contains 396 pages of handwritten text in it, and she confirmed that, indeed, this diary consists of 396 pages. And we see, again, her signature here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And do you know if Mrs. Mladic made a similar declaration in the other note-books that were seized in the February 2010 search?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he [sic] did a similar declaration in the other note-books seized this date on 23 February 2010.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can you tell us, then, how did the OTP come to receive the material from this search?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was similar as in previous case. The first -- we were informed about the search that was conducted on 23 February 2010, and the first on -- on 23 March, I believe, 2000 -- 2010, we received a hard drive containing the scanned version of these documents seized in the house of Bosiljka Mladic on 23 February 2010. And, of course, we requested the original material, and we received the original material -- we received this original material in May. In fact, on the 27 April 2010, the original material was received by my colleague from field office in Belgrade, and then material was stored in the field office in material -- in Belgrade, and only my colleague from the field office had direct access to this material. And on the 7 of May, I think, I arrived to Belgrade, and together with my colleague, I made -- additionally checked -- compared the material with the list of the MUP, and we packed the material to the sealed box, and we transported these documents to The Hague. The material arrived to The Hague on the 11th of May, 2010, on the same day I submitted this entire material to our evidence unit here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I think you referred to the 23rd of March when the first MUP scans were received on a hard drive. Is it possible that you meant to refer to the 29th of March? I believe you made a declaration on this matter, although I'm not going to seek to use that with you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, these two days are correct, because on 23 March our field office received the scanned version of the documents, but on 29 March, here in The Hague, our team received -- me, personally -- we received this hard drive containing the scanned material.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Now, when the OTP first received the scanned versions of these note-books, did the scans include one note-book which had been scanned into two separate parts?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This scan -- this MUP scan included, in fact, one note-book which was scanned in two batches. At that time, we didn't know -- we were not sure whether there is one note-book or whether it was two separate note-books, but indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And if you look again at the paper hand-out and at the first item of Table B, 65 ter numbers 6808 and 6809, do these correspond to the two separate parts of what is, in fact, one note-book?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this -- this particular note-book marked here as 65 ter 06808 and 06809 was scanned at the beginning by the Serbian MUP in two batches. This is this note-book, and this note-book is listed in the MUP inventory as note-book number 41. This note-book covered the period 30 December 1991 until 14 February 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you briefly about the other kinds of materials that you mentioned were also taken from the Mladic family house in the second seizure, including some tapes. Do you know how these were handled, and what was the chain of custody for those materials?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was similar like note-books. First, it was on the possession of Serbian MUP. Then, on 27 April 2010, entire material, including the tapes, was handed over to our field investigator in Belgrade. And then on 11 May 2010, I brought entire material, including the tapes, audiotapes, also brought to The Hague and submitted to evidence unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And do you know what, if anything, in general terms, is recorded on those audiotapes?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly, I know what is in the tapes. They are recorded conversation between various people, including Ratko Mladic, including General Tolimir, including President Karadzic and other prominent people from Bosnia-Herzegovina, not only also from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I won't ask you any further about those tapes. I'd like to turn now, though, to methods by which the note-books were authenticated. After the OTP received the first scans of the note-books from the February 2010 search, did you take any steps or conduct any interviews to further authenticate them?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we referring to the search from February 2010 or from search from 2008?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: The search from February 2010.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Regarding this search, we -- we took some steps to authenticate these documents. The first -- first -- I believe the note-books seized at that time.
